blocks.text: It has been observed that nuclei whose atomic numbers are greater than 82 are naturally unstable; they spontaneously emit radiations. Such nuclei are called radioactive, and the emission of radiation is known as natural radioactivity. The radiations are of three types: alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays. Unstable isotopes can also be produced artificially in the laboratory by nuclear reactions, when a stable element is bombarded with high-energy particles such as neutrons, protons, alpha particles or gamma rays, causing it to become unstable and emit radiation. This is called artificial radioactivity, and the radioactive isotopes are named radioisotopes or radionuclides.

Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays travel differently when passed through an electric field (Fig. 12.4). Alpha particles deflect towards the negative plate, showing that they have a positive charge; they are emitted at high speeds, typically a few per cent of the speed of light, but can travel only several centimetres in air because of their large mass. Beta particles deflect towards the positive plate, showing that they have a negative charge; their deflection is more than that of alpha particles, proving that they are lighter. Beta particles are fast-moving electrons with speeds up to 0.9995 of the speed of light. Gamma rays pass through the electric field without deflection, showing that they have no charge; they are electromagnetic radiation consisting of photons, move with the speed of light, and have the highest penetrating power but the lowest ionizing power. The processes of emitting alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays from the nucleus are called alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay.

If a nucleus has too many protons for its neutrons, the electrostatic repulsion becomes greater than the strong nuclear attraction, the nucleus becomes unstable and it emits alpha particles. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, two protons and two neutrons, so in alpha decay the nucleus loses two protons and two neutrons: the atomic number Z decreases by two and the mass number A by four. In general: parent X (A, Z) -> daughter Y (A - 4, Z - 2) + helium-4 (A = 4, Z = 2) ... (12.2). In alpha decay the number of nucleons (A) and the electric charge are conserved. For example, radium-226 emits an alpha particle and decays into radon-222: radium-226 (Z = 88) -> radon-222 (Z = 86) + helium-4 ... (12.3).

blocks.title: Transmutation and Q-value
blocks.text: The change of one element into another, as of radium into radon, is called transmutation. The mass of the parent nucleus is found to be greater than the total mass of the daughter nucleus and the alpha particle, so the total mass-energy (E = mc^2) of the decay products is less than that of the original nuclide; this difference in mass-energy is called the disintegration energy Q, or the Q-value of the decay.

There are two types of beta decay, beta-minus and beta-plus. (i) Beta-minus decay: some nuclides have a neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) that is too large. The beta particles are not orbital electrons; they are created within the nucleus at the moment of emission: a neutron decays into a proton and an electron, plus an antineutrino, the antiparticle of the neutrino (symbol nu-bar): n -> p + e- + nu-bar. To conserve charge, the change of a neutron into a proton is accompanied by the emission of an electron, the beta particle, which is indistinguishable from an orbital electron. The neutrino and antineutrino have zero charge and very small mass, so they are very hard to observe. No nucleons are lost, so the mass number A stays the same while the atomic number Z increases by one: X (A, Z) -> Y (A, Z + 1) + e- + nu-bar. For example, an unstable thorium isotope decays into protactinium-234 (Z = 91) by beta emission. (The print writes 'the total number of nucleons A remains the same but the mass number Z changes', meaning the atomic number.)

(ii) Beta-plus decay: nuclides with a neutron-to-proton ratio too small for stability decay by emitting a positron instead of an electron. The positron has the same mass as the electron but a positive charge; it is the electron's antiparticle. A proton in the nucleus decays into a neutron and a positron, plus a neutrino: X (A, Z) -> Y (A, Z - 1) + e+ + nu. An example is neon-19 decaying into fluorine-19 by emitting a positron and a neutrino. The neutrino was first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930 to preserve energy conservation in beta decay; in 1953 it was detected by F. Reines and C. L. Cowan in a high-power nuclear reactor, and Reines received the Nobel Prize in 1995 (For Your Information).

blocks.caption: Radioactivity: alpha, beta and gamma radiation and their energy spectra (original diagram after Figures 12.4 to 12.6 and topic 12.4).
blocks.long_description: Between charged plates the three radiations separate: alpha particles, positive and heavy, bend slightly towards the negative plate; beta particles, negative and light, bend strongly towards the positive plate; gamma rays, uncharged, go straight. Alpha decay lowers the atomic number by two and the mass number by four; beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, raising the atomic number by one with an electron and an antineutrino emitted; beta-plus decay turns a proton into a neutron with a positron and a neutrino; gamma decay leaves both numbers unchanged. Alpha particles from one nuclide all have the same energy, giving separate lines, while beta particles share their energy with a neutrino and so have every energy from zero up to a maximum.

blocks.text: Energy of alpha and beta particles

In both alpha decay and beta decay of a particular radionuclide, the same amount of energy is released. In alpha decay of a particular radionuclide every emitted alpha particle has the same sharply defined kinetic energy: when the number of alpha particles is plotted against kinetic energy, distinct spikes appear (Fig. 12.5), showing that alpha particles have discrete energies. In beta emission, however, the energy is shared between the beta particle and the antineutrino in varying proportions; the sum of the electron's (or positron's) energy and the antineutrino's (or neutrino's) energy stays the same in every case. Thus in beta decay the energy of an electron or positron may range from zero to a maximum value: the graph is a continuous curve (Fig. 12.6), showing that beta particles have a continuous range of energies. Conservation of momentum and energy applies in both alpha and beta emission.
The emission of gamma radiation from a nucleus is represented as X* (A, Z) -> X (A, Z) + gamma radiation, where X* is an excited nucleus and X the ground state of the nucleus; A and Z do not change.

blocks.prompt: Fill in the missing particle or nucleus: (a) calcium-45 (Z = 20) -> ? + e- + nu-bar; (b) excited copper-58 (Z = 29) -> ? + gamma (short question 12.4). Uranium-238 is an alpha emitter and polonium-218 (Z = 84) a beta-minus emitter; find the daughters (numerical 12.1, 12.2).
blocks.explanation: (a) Beta-minus decay raises Z by one and keeps A: scandium-45 (Z = 21). (b) Gamma decay changes neither: copper-58 (Z = 29) in its ground state. Uranium-238 (Z = 92) loses 4 nucleons and 2 protons: A = 234, Z = 90, thorium-234. Polonium-218 gains a proton: A = 218, Z = 85, astatine-218.

blocks.prompt: Why does beta decay have a continuous energy spectrum while alpha decay has a discrete one (short question 12.11; constructed response 12.1)? Why must a neutrino be released in positron emission (short question 12.5)?
blocks.explanation: In alpha decay only two bodies share the released energy, the alpha particle and the daughter nucleus, so conservation of momentum fixes each one's share and every alpha has the same energy. In beta decay three bodies share it, the electron (or positron), the antineutrino (or neutrino) and the daughter nucleus, and the split varies from decay to decay, so the beta particle can have any energy from zero to the maximum. Without the neutrino, energy, momentum and angular momentum (spin) would not balance in positron emission; the neutrino carries off the missing energy and spin and conserves lepton number.

items: Natural radioactivity: nuclei with Z above 82 emit alpha, beta and gamma radiation; artificial radioactivity makes radioisotopes. In an electric field alpha bends slightly to the - plate, beta strongly to the + plate, gamma not at all.

Alpha: Z - 2, A - 4 (radium-226 -> radon-222 + helium-4); transmutation; Q-value. Beta-minus: n -> p + e- + nu-bar, Z + 1. Beta-plus: p -> n + e+ + nu, Z - 1 (neon-19 -> fluorine-19). Gamma: X* -> X + gamma. Alpha energies discrete, beta continuous. Table 12.2 compares the three.
